practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is NOT one of the four segmentation bases in the specification?
A) Age
B) Gender
C) Personality
D) Income
practice_questions.marks: C) Personality [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘market segmentation’.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for a basic definition (e.g. ‘splitting the market into groups’).
2 marks for a clear, accurate definition (e.g. ‘splitting a market into smaller groups of customers who share similar characteristics such as age, gender, income or location’).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why a clothing retailer might segment its market by age.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for identifying a valid reason (e.g. different age groups want different styles, have different spending power, use different media).
2 marks for a developed point (e.g. teenagers want on-trend fast fashion while older customers want classic, durable pieces).
3 marks for a fully developed point with a consequence for the business (e.g. … so designing separate ranges and adverts for each age group means marketing spend is focused on people who will actually buy, raising the return on every pound spent).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A sportswear brand spends £180,000 on marketing. It targets 4 segments and splits its budget equally between them. Calculate how much is spent on each segment.
practice_questions.marks:
£180,000 ÷ 4 = £45,000 per segment.
1 mark for correct method (÷ 4).
2 marks for correct working shown.
3 marks for correct final answer of £45,000 with £ sign.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how identifying customer needs could benefit a new UK coffee shop opening in a student town.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Sustained analysis across two or more linked benefits, applied to the coffee shop context, with clear chains of reasoning (e.g. identifying that students want cheap drinks, fast Wi-Fi and late opening → lets the shop design the correct marketing mix → which means marketing spend is focused on people who will buy → which reduces the risk of costly mistakes like overstocking premium beans nobody wants).
Secure (3–4): Two relevant benefits identified and explained with some application to the coffee shop.
Developing (2): One benefit explained in general terms; limited application.
Emerging (1): Basic point with no application.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: ‘Segmenting by income is always the best way for a UK supermarket to target customers.’ Evaluate this statement. You should use at least one named UK business in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments for:
• Aldi’s entire business model is built on income segmentation — low prices target cost-conscious shoppers, which drove record UK market share.
• Income segmentation affects every element of the mix: store fit-out, own-brand ranges, advertising tone.
• It makes the target customer easy to identify and measure through census data.

Arguments against:
• Waitrose shows that high-income segmentation works too, but both can be wrong for other shops — Tesco segments by age and location (Express stores in cities vs Extra in suburbs).
• Location often matters more than income — a premium store in a low-income area will fail regardless of pricing.
• Combining bases (age + income + location) usually produces better targeting than any single base.

Mastering (10–12): Sustained two-sided argument with named UK businesses, clear chains of reasoning, and a justified conclusion.
Secure (7–9): Balanced argument with some application and a conclusion.
Developing (4–6): Some argument on one or both sides; limited application or conclusion.
Emerging (1–3): Simple points; no real evaluation.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the best definition of flow production?
A) Making one item at a time for a specific customer
B) Making large volumes of identical items on a continuous line
C) Making small batches then switching machines for the next batch
D) Making items only once a customer order arrives
practice_questions.marks: B) Making large volumes of identical items on a continuous line [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘just in time (JIT)’.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (2): A stock-management method where materials and parts are delivered from suppliers exactly when they are needed for production, so almost no stock is held on site.
Secure (1): A method of receiving stock only when it is needed / holding very little stock.
Emerging (0): Vague or incorrect — e.g. ‘when things arrive on time’.

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage for a small bespoke furniture maker of using job production rather than flow production.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): A clear advantage with a developed chain of reasoning — e.g. Job production lets the maker customise every piece to the customer’s measurements and taste (1), which means the business can charge a premium price because each item feels unique (2), boosting profit margins even though output is low (3).
Secure (2): A clear advantage with some development but the reasoning stops short.
Developing (1): A valid advantage identified but not explained.
Emerging (0): No valid advantage or confuses with flow production.

practice_questions.text: A bakery uses flow production. Fixed costs per week are £4,800 and variable costs are £0.40 per loaf. The bakery produces 12,000 loaves per week. Calculate the total cost per loaf.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): Fixed cost per loaf = 4,800 ÷ 12,000 = £0.40 (1). Total cost per loaf = 0.40 + 0.40 = £0.80 (2). Correct answer with units and working shown (3).
Secure (2): Correct method shown but a slip in the arithmetic or missing units.
Developing (1): One correct step (e.g. calculates fixed cost per loaf) but fails to add variable cost.
Emerging (0): No valid method. Method marks are awarded even if the final figure is wrong, so working must be shown.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on Nissan’s Sunderland car plant of using just-in-time (JIT) stock management.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): A developed chain of reasoning, applied to Nissan, drawing on more than one factor. E.g. JIT means parts arrive at the line hour by hour, so Nissan needs far less warehouse space and ties up less cash in stock, freeing capital for investment in the plant. However, the plant becomes vulnerable — a Channel ferry delay or supplier strike could halt production within hours because no buffer stock exists. The net effect is lower running costs in normal conditions but much higher risk when supply chains are disrupted, as seen during recent semiconductor shortages.
Secure (3–4): Clear analysis of at least one impact with some development, applied to Nissan.
Developing (1–2): Identifies effects but reasoning is limited or not applied to the context.
Emerging (0): No valid impact or purely generic points.

practice_questions.text: Anya owns a growing cake business that currently makes one bespoke cake at a time. She is deciding whether to stay with job production or move to a flow-production line making a standard range of three cakes. Justify which method she should choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9): A clear decision supported by two developed reasons, weighed against the alternative, with context applied throughout. E.g. Anya should stay with job production because customers pay premium prices for bespoke cakes — moving to flow would require heavy investment in machinery and kill her unique selling point. Flow production would cut unit costs but she would lose the customisation that brings customers in. Her best route is to keep job production while using some lean techniques to reduce waste.
Secure (5–7): A clear judgement with at least two reasons but uneven development, or limited weighing of the alternative.
Developing (3–4): Some reasons listed on both sides but no real judgement.
Emerging (1–2): Describes the methods without choosing or justifying.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an internal source of finance?
A) Bank loan
B) Retained profit
C) Overdraft
D) Government grant
practice_questions.marks: B) Retained profit [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘trade credit’.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for a basic definition (e.g. ‘paying a supplier later’).
2 marks for a clear, accurate definition (e.g. ‘an arrangement where a supplier delivers goods now and allows the business to pay after an agreed period, typically 30, 60 or 90 days’).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one disadvantage of using a bank loan to buy new equipment.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for identifying a valid disadvantage (e.g. interest must be paid, collateral required, fixed repayments).
2 marks for a developed point (e.g. the business must pay interest on top of the amount borrowed, which raises the overall cost of the equipment).
3 marks for a fully developed point with a consequence (e.g. … which reduces monthly profit and may leave the business short of cash if sales dip below forecast).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A start-up needs £60,000 of finance. The owner provides £15,000 of savings, takes a bank loan of £35,000 and receives a government grant for the rest. Calculate the value of the grant.
practice_questions.marks:
£60,000 − £15,000 − £35,000 = £10,000.
1 mark for correct method (subtracting savings and loan from total).
2 marks for correct working shown.
3 marks for correct final answer of £10,000 with £ sign.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse why retained profit may be a better source of finance than a bank loan for an established UK business wanting to open a new shop.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Sustained analysis of two linked reasons applied to the established business context, with clear chains of reasoning (e.g. retained profit has no interest cost → so all profit from the new shop stays inside the business → which improves long-term profit margin → and there is no risk of the bank demanding repayment if sales slow).
Secure (3–4): Two relevant reasons identified and explained with some application.
Developing (2): One reason explained in general terms; limited application.
Emerging (1): Basic point, no development.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: A new independent bakery in Manchester needs £40,000 to buy ovens and pay its first six months of rent. Justify whether the owner should use a bank loan or a new share issue to raise the money.
practice_questions.marks:
Bank loan arguments:
• Available to sole traders and partnerships (a new bakery is likely a sole trader).
• Owner keeps full control of the business.
• Fixed repayments allow clear budgeting.

New share issue arguments:
• No repayment pressure, no interest.
• Usually only available to Ltds and plcs, not sole traders — likely rules it out.
• Dilutes ownership and control.

Mastering (7–9): Clear recommendation (bank loan) with two developed reasons, weighing against the other option, and recognising the legal-structure barrier to share issues.
Secure (4–6): Recommendation with some reasoning on both sides.
Developing (2–3): One-sided argument with a weak judgement.
Emerging (1): Simple preference, no real reasoning.
[9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a factor of production classed as capital?
A) A delivery driver
B) A pizza oven in a Domino's kitchen
C) A farmer's field
D) The entrepreneur who founded the business
practice_questions.marks:
B) A pizza oven in a Domino's kitchen [1 mark]
Other options describe labour (A), land (C) and enterprise (D).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'opportunity cost'.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: the cost of a choice / what is given up when a decision is made.
2 marks: a fuller definition referring to the value of the next best alternative that is given up when a choice is made.
Acceptable example: 'If a business spends £10,000 on new signage, the opportunity cost might be the marketing campaign that money could have paid for instead.' [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why someone might choose to become an entrepreneur rather than work for an employer.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a reason (e.g. to be their own boss, flexible hours, pursue an interest, spot a gap in the market, earn more money, dissatisfaction with current job).
2 marks: adds a 'because' clause explaining the reason.
3 marks: links the reason to a specific benefit for the entrepreneur.
Indicative answer: 'An entrepreneur might start a business to be their own boss (1). This means they can make decisions about products and working hours without needing approval (2), which gives them a sense of control that an employee would not have in a large firm like Tesco (3).' [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how two characteristics of an entrepreneur might help a new food-delivery business succeed in its first year.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two characteristics chosen, each developed into a full chain of reasoning that links to a first-year business outcome (e.g. willingness to take risk → tries new delivery area → builds customer base ahead of rivals).
Secure: Two characteristics chosen and explained, with at least one chain reaching a business impact.
Developing: Two characteristics identified with some explanation but limited linkage to the business context.
Emerging: Lists characteristics without explanation or context.
Indicative content: hard-working (long hours in the launch phase), innovative (new menu or delivery model), organised (managing cash and rotas), willing to take risk (borrowing to start up). Chains should land on a first-year outcome such as faster break-even, customer loyalty, or avoiding failure. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: A school leaver has £8,000 saved and is choosing between (A) opening a mobile car-valeting business or (B) spending the money on a full-time college course. Justify which option you would recommend.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear recommendation supported by at least two developed reasons (one fully explained), weighed against the rejected option, with explicit reference to opportunity cost and the applicant's circumstances.
Secure: Clear recommendation with two developed reasons, some comparison, some reference to opportunity cost.
Developing: Recommendation with reasons but limited comparison or evaluation.
Emerging: Lists pros and cons of each option without making a supported recommendation.
Indicative content for A: immediate income, becomes their own boss, builds enterprise skills; risk of failure, long hours, small market. For B: higher long-term earnings, qualifications open more careers; delays income, £8,000 opportunity cost of not starting a business. A strong answer names the opportunity cost of whichever option is rejected. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The main reason people start a business is to make money.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should give reasoned arguments to support and challenge the statement and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments to support: profit is the reward for risk-taking; higher earnings than an employee can achieve; financial security for the owner's family; attracts investors and lenders; BrewDog and Gymshark founders scaled precisely because they chased profit.
Arguments to challenge: many entrepreneurs are motivated by independence, flexibility, passion for an interest, or dissatisfaction with their current job; social enterprises like The Big Issue exist to benefit others; many early-stage founders accept low pay for years; non-financial satisfaction can drive longer commitment than money alone.

Mastering: Balanced argument with developed points on both sides, applied to real or realistic businesses, and a judgement that introduces a new weighting (e.g. 'it depends on the stage of the business' or 'money is necessary but not sufficient').
Secure: Balanced argument with developed points both sides and a clear conclusion.
Developing: Some points on both sides, limited development, conclusion restates earlier points.
Emerging: One-sided argument or list of points without evaluation. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a flat organisational structure?
A) Many layers of management and narrow spans of control
B) Few layers of management and wide spans of control
C) All decisions taken at head office
D) No chain of command at all
practice_questions.marks:
B) Few layers of management and wide spans of control [1 mark]

Mastering: Correct answer selected.
Emerging: Incorrect answer.

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘span of control’.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (2 marks): Clear definition — the number of employees a manager is directly responsible for / directly supervises.
Secure (1 mark): Basic idea of ‘how many people a manager looks after’ without precise wording.
Emerging (0 marks): Vague or incorrect reference (e.g. ‘how the business is controlled’).

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit for a small technology start-up of having a flat organisational structure.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3 marks): Clear benefit identified (e.g. fast decision-making) + explanation with a ‘because’ clause (fewer layers means instructions travel quickly) + linked to a start-up context (important when competing against larger rivals).
Secure (2 marks): Benefit identified and explained but not applied to a start-up.
Developing (1 mark): Benefit named without explanation.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant point.

practice_questions.text: A bank has 5 senior managers, each responsible for 8 branch managers. After delayering, 2 senior manager posts are removed and their branches are shared equally among the remaining 3. Calculate the new average span of control for the 3 remaining senior managers. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3 marks): Total branch managers = 5 × 8 = 40. New span = 40 ÷ 3 = 13.33 (accept 13.3 or 13).
Secure (2 marks): Correct total (40) found but arithmetic slip in the division.
Developing (1 mark): Some correct working shown (e.g. spotted 40 branch managers) but no final answer.
Emerging (0 marks): No valid working.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a large supermarket chain of moving from a centralised to a decentralised structure.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Two developed chains of reasoning, e.g. local managers can respond to local tastes (ethnic food ranges, seasonal stock) which raises sales and customer loyalty; however, brand consistency may weaken, because each store decides differently, which could confuse shoppers.
Secure (3–4 marks): One fully developed chain or two partial chains. Some application to a supermarket.
Developing (1–2 marks): Relevant points but mostly a list, little development.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant analysis.

practice_questions.text: A growing e-commerce business currently has a tall structure with 6 layers of management. The CEO is considering delayering to 3 layers. Justify whether or not the CEO should delayer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–9 marks): Two developed reasons supporting the chosen option (one fully explained) — e.g. faster communication in online markets, lower wage costs. Weighed against at least one counter-argument (redundancies harm morale; overloaded remaining managers). Clear, supported judgement.
Secure (4–6 marks): Some development of both sides. Judgement present but brief.
Developing (1–3 marks): Mainly a list of pros and cons. Limited or no judgement.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes e-commerce?
A) Selling goods only in physical shops
B) Buying and selling goods and services using the internet
C) Advertising a business on television
D) Training staff using online videos
practice_questions.marks: B) Buying and selling goods and services using the internet [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘digital communication’.
practice_questions.marks:
The use of digital tools (such as email, social media, messaging apps or video calls) [1 mark] to share information between a business and its stakeholders [1 mark].

Mastering: precise definition using correct business vocabulary.
Secure: accurate meaning with one clear example.
Developing: partial meaning, example missing or vague.
Emerging: definition incorrect or confused with a related term.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way in which e-commerce can reduce costs for a small UK fashion retailer.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• Identification: e-commerce removes the need to rent a high-street shop [1 mark].
• Development: the retailer saves on rent, business rates and shop-floor staffing costs [1 mark].
• Reasoning: the money saved can be reinvested in stock, marketing or a wider product range, which can raise sales without raising fixed costs [1 mark].

Mastering: identification, development AND a 'because' chain of reasoning.
Secure: identification and clear development.
Developing: correct identification with limited development.
Emerging: vague or incorrect point about e-commerce.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact of social media on a small independent café that has just opened in a city centre.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (accept developed reasoning that draws on one or more factors):
• Low-cost marketing: free Instagram and TikTok posts reach local customers for no spend, which raises awareness and footfall, leading to higher revenue in the early months when budgets are tight.
• Two-way communication: customers can leave reviews and tag the café, creating social proof that attracts new visitors — but negative reviews can spread just as quickly and damage reputation before the owner can respond.
• Data and engagement: insights on which posts perform well helps the owner refine menu photos and offers, which improves conversion from followers to paying customers.
• Risk of overreliance: if the café depends on one platform and an algorithm changes, visibility can drop overnight.

Mastering: developed chains of reasoning using two or more factors, applied to the café, with clear impact on the business.
Secure: a developed chain on one factor plus a supporting point, applied to the café.
Developing: relevant points listed with limited development or weak application.
Emerging: generic statements about social media with no application.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A small bookshop is deciding between two options to grow sales:
Option 1 — Launch an e-commerce website with UK-wide delivery.
Option 2 — Expand marketing through a paid social-media campaign for the existing shop.
Justify which option the bookshop should choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
Option 1 (e-commerce):
• Opens a nationwide market, not limited to local footfall, so potential revenue is far higher.
• Allows the shop to trade 24/7, including overnight and weekends.
• Drawback: set-up costs for a website, payment systems, packaging and couriers; returns eat into margin.
Option 2 (paid social-media campaign):
• Cheaper to start — a few hundred pounds can reach thousands locally.
• Builds on an existing loyal customer base and drives repeat visits.
• Drawback: still limited to people within travelling distance of the shop.

Justification must choose one option and weigh it against the other. A strong answer might argue e-commerce is worth the investment because local footfall is finite and books are easy to package; or argue that the paid campaign is safer first because the shop has no online experience and cash flow is tight.

Mastering: clear decision with two developed reasons for the chosen option, weighed against the rejected option, applied to the bookshop.
Secure: decision with one developed reason plus a supporting point and some weighing.
Developing: decision stated with limited reasoning or weak weighing of the alternative.
Emerging: lists pros and cons of both options with no clear decision.
[9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘All UK high-street retailers should shift most of their sales online.’
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
Arguments in support:
• Online sales allow 24/7 trading and a national or global customer base, which can raise revenue far beyond what a single high-street unit can achieve.
• Fixed costs fall — fewer shops means less rent, rates and staffing.
• Data on customer behaviour helps retailers target marketing and personalise offers, increasing conversion.
• Companies that did not adapt, like BHS and Debenhams, collapsed partly because they relied too heavily on physical stores.

Arguments against:
• Many products — fresh food, clothes needing try-on, high-value items — still sell better in store, where customers touch, try and ask questions.
• E-commerce has its own costs: warehousing, couriers, returns, cyber-security.
• Shutting shops damages community presence, staff relationships and brand image.
• ‘Most’ is a strong word — an integrated strategy (click-and-collect, flagship stores plus online) often works better than going mainly online.

Conclusion should introduce a new weighting: for example, it depends on the type of product and the target customer. Fashion and electronics suit a heavy online tilt; fresh food and premium services may not. The most important factor is knowing where the retailer's customers prefer to buy.

Mastering: balanced argument with two developed points on each side, a justified conclusion that introduces a new weighting (‘it depends on...’ or ‘the most important factor is...’).
Secure: balanced argument with some development and a clear conclusion.
Developing: one-sided argument or a conclusion that only summarises earlier points.
Emerging: brief points with no real evaluation or conclusion.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of secondary research?
A) Running a focus group of 10 teenagers
B) Reading an ONS report on household spending
C) Interviewing customers outside a shop
D) Sending a questionnaire to 500 new customers
practice_questions.marks: B) Reading an ONS report on household spending [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two examples of primary market research methods.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark per correct method, up to 2.
Accept: questionnaires, surveys, interviews, focus groups, observation, customer trials.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit to Tesco of using its Clubcard to collect market research data.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for a valid benefit (e.g. collects quantitative data, tracks customer buying habits, cheap compared to new surveys).
2 marks for development (e.g. Clubcard tracks exactly what each customer buys and how often).
3 marks for a developed point with a consequence (e.g. … so Tesco can personalise offers, predict demand and reduce waste, increasing profit and customer loyalty).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A new bakery sells £120,000 of bread in a local market worth £1,500,000. Calculate the bakery’s market share.
practice_questions.marks:
Market share = (120,000 ÷ 1,500,000) × 100 = 8%.
1 mark for correct formula/method.
2 marks for correct substitution and working.
3 marks for correct final answer of 8% with % sign.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a small independent UK coffee shop could benefit from using both primary and secondary research before launch.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Sustained analysis of both primary and secondary methods with clear chains of reasoning applied to a small coffee shop (e.g. secondary: check Google Maps for local rivals → quick, free measure of competition → informs location decision; primary: survey 50 locals on price → reveals willingness to pay → sets menu prices and reduces risk of pricing too high).
Secure (3–4): Two benefits identified, one from each type; some application.
Developing (2): One benefit explained; limited application.
Emerging (1): Basic point with no application.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Sainsbury’s is considering launching a new range of plant-based ready meals. Justify ONE market research method they could use to help the launch.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–9): Clear justified recommendation, sustained analysis of chosen method and why it beats alternatives, applied to Sainsbury’s (e.g. focus groups of 8–10 vegan/flexitarian shoppers to taste prototypes → qualitative data on flavour and packaging → reveals which flavours to launch — beats a questionnaire which cannot capture real taste reactions).
Secure (5–6): Method identified with reasons, some comparison and application.
Developing (3–4): Method chosen with limited reasoning and minimal comparison.
Emerging (1–2): Simple point; no justification or comparison.
[9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following types of business has unlimited liability?
A) Public limited company (Plc)
B) Private limited company (Ltd)
C) Sole trader
D) Registered charity
practice_questions.marks:
C) Sole trader [1 mark]
Plcs and Ltds have limited liability; registered charities operate under separate charity law.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'limited liability'.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: shareholders can only lose a limited amount / protects the owners.
2 marks: shareholders can only lose the amount they invested in the company — their personal assets are protected if the company goes bust. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage for a growing family bakery of becoming a private limited company rather than remaining a sole trader.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies an advantage (limited liability, easier to raise finance from invited shareholders, separate legal identity, continuity if an owner leaves).
2 marks: a 'because' clause explains it.
3 marks: links to the specific bakery context.
Indicative answer: 'Becoming an Ltd gives the owners limited liability (1), meaning if the bakery failed they would only lose the money they invested, not their family home (2). This matters as the bakery takes on bigger supplier contracts where the financial risk is higher (3).' [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how unlimited liability could affect the decisions made by the owner of a small mobile car-wash business.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed chains of reasoning that trace unlimited liability → owner decision → business consequence, applied to the car-wash context.
Secure: Two chains, one fully developed, relevant to the context.
Developing: Identifies effects with partial development, limited application.
Emerging: Defines unlimited liability without linking it to decisions.
Indicative chains: (1) avoids borrowing large sums → can't afford a second van → growth slower than rivals; (2) takes out personal insurance to protect house → extra cost eats into profit → may raise prices; (3) avoids hiring staff → keeps business small → limits revenue. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Two friends are launching an online fashion brand. Justify whether they should begin as a partnership or as a private limited company.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear recommendation with two developed reasons (one fully explained), weighed against the alternative, applied to an online fashion context with reference to limited liability and finance needs.
Secure: Clear recommendation, two developed reasons, some comparison.
Developing: Recommendation with reasons but limited weighting.
Emerging: Lists features of both without a supported recommendation.
Indicative content for Partnership: cheap to set up, simple, shared decisions, profits split as agreed; unlimited liability is a concern because fashion stock can go out of date fast. For Ltd: limited liability protects them if unsold stock creates debt; can sell shares to family/friends for launch capital; more admin and filing costs. A strong answer lands on limited liability as the critical factor for a stock-heavy online business. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Every growing business should aim to become a public limited company.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should give reasoned arguments to support and challenge the statement and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments to support: huge access to finance through share issues (e.g. JD Sports expansion); limited liability; raised brand profile; separate legal identity gives stability; ability to attract top management via share options.
Arguments to challenge: loss of control as ownership diluted across thousands of shareholders; vulnerability to hostile takeovers; pressure to deliver short-term profits for the stock market; costly reporting and compliance; many successful UK businesses (Dyson, Specsavers) stay as Ltds deliberately; a small local cafe has no need for Plc-scale finance.

Mastering: Balanced argument with developed points both sides, applied to real examples, and a judgement that introduces a new weighting (e.g. 'depends on the size and finance needs of the business').
Secure: Balanced argument with development on both sides and a clear conclusion.
Developing: Some points either side with limited development.
Emerging: One-sided list with no evaluation. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes just-in-case (JIC) stock management?
A) Ordering stock only after the customer has paid
B) Keeping spare buffer stock so demand can always be met
C) Sending stock back to the supplier each evening
D) Holding no stock at all
practice_questions.marks: B) Keeping spare buffer stock so demand can always be met [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two factors that affect a business’s choice of supplier.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (2): Any two from — price, quality, reliability (1 mark each, up to 2). Other accepted factors: location, delivery speed, ethical/environmental credentials, payment terms.
Secure (1): One correct factor identified.
Emerging (0): No valid factor, or vague terms like ‘good ones’.

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit to a UK supermarket chain of managing an effective supply chain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): A clear benefit with a developed ‘because’ chain — e.g. An effective supply chain means fresh produce moves from farm to shelf quickly (1), which reduces wastage from food spoilage (2), cutting costs and protecting profit margins while keeping shelves fully stocked for customers (3).
Secure (2): Benefit stated with some development.
Developing (1): Benefit identified without explanation.
Emerging (0): No valid benefit.

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer buys 8,000 components at £3.50 each. The supplier offers a 5% bulk discount if the order is placed in a single delivery. Calculate the cost saving the bulk discount provides.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): Original total cost = 8,000 × 3.50 = £28,000 (1). Discount = 28,000 × 0.05 = £1,400 (2). Saving = £1,400 with units shown (3).
Secure (2): Correct method but arithmetic slip or missing units.
Developing (1): Calculates one step only.
Emerging (0): No valid method. Method marks are awarded even if the final figure is wrong, so working must be shown.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a UK supermarket chain of switching from just-in-case (JIC) to just-in-time (JIT) stock management.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): A developed chain of reasoning drawing on multiple factors. E.g. Switching to JIT would free up warehouse space and reduce cash tied up in stock, giving the supermarket capital to invest in stores or digital systems. However, supermarkets depend on predictable shelf availability — if a haulage strike delays deliveries, whole ranges disappear within hours, pushing customers to competitors. The efficiency saving is real but so is the brand damage if shelves empty. A pure JIT model therefore carries more risk for a supermarket than for a factory where production can simply pause.
Secure (3–4): Clear analysis of at least one impact with some development.
Developing (1–2): Identifies an effect without developing reasoning or applying context.
Emerging (0): No valid impact identified.

practice_questions.text: Priya runs a small mail-order skincare business. She is choosing between two suppliers: Supplier A is 10% cheaper but has missed two deliveries in the past year; Supplier B is 10% more expensive but has a perfect delivery record. Justify which supplier Priya should choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9): A clear decision with two developed reasons weighed against the alternative, applied to Priya’s context. E.g. Priya should choose Supplier B. Her customers rely on mail-order, so a missed delivery directly means empty shelves and refunded orders — damaging her reputation in a way the 10% saving cannot recover. Reliability protects revenue and customer loyalty; Supplier A’s cheaper price is a false economy because every missed delivery cancels several weeks of savings. The 10% extra from Supplier B is best seen as an insurance premium.
Secure (5–7): A clear judgement with two reasons but uneven development, or limited handling of the alternative.
Developing (3–4): Reasons on both sides but no committed judgement.
Emerging (1–2): Describes the options without choosing.

practice_questions.text:

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘person specification’.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (2 marks): Clear definition — a document listing the skills, qualifications and personal qualities an ideal candidate should have.
Secure (1 mark): Basic idea (e.g. ‘describes the ideal candidate’) without precise detail.
Emerging (0 marks): Vague reference (e.g. ‘describes the job’) — this is a job description, not a person specification.

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit to John Lewis of filling a store manager vacancy using internal recruitment.

Mastering (3 marks): Benefit identified (e.g. shorter induction / cheaper) + ‘because’ clause (the partner already knows John Lewis’s customer-service culture) + applied to the John Lewis context (partners motivated by a visible promotion path).
Secure (2 marks): Benefit identified and explained but generic.
Developing (1 mark): Benefit named only.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant point.

practice_questions.text: A café hires a new full-time employee. Advert cost £120, interview time costs £60, and induction training costs £320. Calculate the total cost of hiring this employee. Show your working.

Mastering (3 marks): £120 + £60 + £320 = £500. Correct working shown, units included.
Secure (2 marks): Correct answer (£500) but no working shown, or working shown with an arithmetic slip.
Developing (1 mark): Some correct working or correctly totals two of the three figures.
Emerging (0 marks): No valid working.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a hospitality business of using zero-hour contracts for its kitchen staff.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Two developed chains of reasoning, e.g. flexibility to match staff to demand lowers wage costs and protects cash flow during quiet weeks, which helps survival; however, staff may feel insecure, leading to low motivation, poor food quality and higher turnover.
Secure (3–4 marks): One fully developed chain or two partial chains, some application to hospitality.
Developing (1–2 marks): Listed points with little development.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant analysis.

practice_questions.text: A growing technology start-up has a senior engineering vacancy. The founders are choosing between promoting an internal junior engineer or hiring an experienced external candidate. Justify which option the founders should choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–9 marks): Two developed reasons for the chosen option (one fully explained) — e.g. external hire brings specialist AI experience the junior lacks, raising product quality quickly. Weighed against at least one counter (loses motivational power of internal promotion; longer induction). Clear, supported judgement, e.g. start-up needs skills fast so external hire is justified despite the cost.
Secure (4–6 marks): Some development of both options. Judgement present but brief.
Developing (1–3 marks): Mainly listing pros and cons, limited judgement.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the best example of sustainable business practice?
A) A supermarket opening a new out-of-town store
B) A clothing retailer sourcing cotton from certified sustainable farms
C) A takeaway switching to single-use plastic containers
D) A courier firm replacing bicycles with diesel vans
practice_questions.marks: B) A clothing retailer sourcing cotton from certified sustainable farms [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘trade-off’ in the context of ethical decisions.
practice_questions.marks:
A situation where a business must give up something in one area [1 mark] to gain a benefit in another, for example paying higher wages (cost) to improve staff loyalty (gain) [1 mark].

Mastering: precise definition with a relevant business example.
Secure: accurate meaning with a general example.
Developing: partial meaning, example missing.
Emerging: confused or incorrect definition.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way a coffee chain can reduce its environmental impact.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• Identification: offer a discount for customers using reusable cups [1 mark].
• Development: fewer disposable cups are used, reducing waste sent to landfill [1 mark].
• Reasoning: because less packaging is produced and bought, the firm also cuts raw-material costs and builds a reputation for sustainability, which can attract eco-conscious customers [1 mark].

Mastering: identification, development AND a ‘because’ chain of reasoning.
Secure: identification and clear development.
Developing: correct identification with limited development.
Emerging: vague or incorrect point.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a UK fashion retailer of adopting a more ethical supply chain.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (accept developed reasoning that draws on one or more factors):
• Higher costs: paying above-minimum wages and auditing factories raises unit costs, which may squeeze profit margins in the short term.
• Brand reputation: ethical sourcing can be promoted in marketing, attracting eco-conscious customers and supporting premium prices, which raises revenue.
• Staff loyalty: ethical firms often find it easier to recruit and keep staff, reducing training costs.
• Risk reduction: auditing suppliers avoids scandals (e.g. Boohoo 2020) that damage reputation and share price.
• Trade-off: short-term profit versus long-term loyalty — the net effect depends on how quickly customers respond.

Mastering: developed chains of reasoning using two or more factors, applied to a fashion retailer.
Secure: a developed chain on one factor plus a supporting point, applied.
Developing: relevant points listed with limited development or weak application.
Emerging: generic statements about ethics with no application.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A medium-sized chocolate manufacturer is choosing between two options to respond to customer pressure on sustainability:
Option 1 — Switch to fully recyclable packaging, raising packaging costs by 8%.
Option 2 — Invest in solar panels on factory roofs, funded by a bank loan.
Justify which option the manufacturer should choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
Option 1 (recyclable packaging):
• Visible to customers on every bar — easy to promote and build brand image.
• Responds directly to current consumer pressure.
• Drawback: an 8% rise in packaging cost squeezes margin; may require a price rise.
Option 2 (solar panels):
• Reduces energy bills long term, improving profit once installed.
• Cuts carbon emissions, protecting against future regulation.
• Drawback: loan repayments strain cash flow; payback period may be several years; invisible to customers unless marketed.

Justification must pick one option and weigh it against the other. A strong answer could argue that recyclable packaging is the better short-term move because it is visible to customers and responds to current pressure, while solar panels can be phased in later from retained profit. A different strong answer could argue solar panels deliver larger long-term savings.

Mastering: clear decision with two developed reasons, weighed against the rejected option, applied to the manufacturer.
Secure: decision with one developed reason, supporting point, and some weighing.
Developing: decision stated with limited reasoning or weak weighing.
Emerging: lists pros and cons of both options with no clear decision.
[9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘Ethical behaviour always reduces a business’s profits.’
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
Arguments in support:
• Ethical decisions often raise costs — fair-trade ingredients, higher wages, audited supply chains — squeezing margins.
• Sustainable packaging and cleaner technology require upfront investment before any returns.
• If rivals do not follow suit, ethical firms can be undercut on price.

Arguments against:
• Strong ethical reputation builds customer loyalty, allowing premium pricing (e.g. Patagonia, Tony’s Chocolonely).
• Ethical firms avoid scandals that wipe billions off share prices — Volkswagen (2015), Boohoo (2020).
• Ethical firms attract and retain better staff, cutting recruitment and training costs.
• Early compliance with future regulation avoids scramble and fines later.

Conclusion should introduce a new weighting — for example, it depends on the time frame and the type of customer. In the short term, ethics can reduce profit; in the long term, it often supports profit. The most important factor is whether customers are willing to pay for ethics.

Mastering: balanced argument with two developed points on each side and a justified conclusion that introduces a new weighting.
Secure: balanced argument with some development and a clear conclusion.
Developing: one-sided argument or conclusion that only summarises earlier points.
Emerging: brief points with no real evaluation or conclusion.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a cash inflow for a retail shop?
A) Paying staff wages
B) Buying new stock
C) A customer paying for goods at the till
D) Paying the monthly rent
practice_questions.marks: C) A customer paying for goods at the till [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give the meaning of the term ‘closing balance’ in a cash-flow forecast.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for a basic answer (e.g. ‘cash at the end of the month’).
2 marks for a clear definition (e.g. ‘the amount of cash the business has at the end of a month, calculated as opening balance plus net cash flow’).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way a business could reduce its cash outflows.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for identifying a valid method (e.g. switch to cheaper suppliers, renegotiate rent, cut non-essential spending, reduce stock levels).
2 marks for a developed point (e.g. switching to a cheaper supplier reduces the cost of every unit of stock bought).
3 marks for a fully developed point with a consequence (e.g. … so monthly cash outflows fall, improving the closing balance and reducing the risk of going overdrawn during a quiet trading month).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A coffee shop has a March opening balance of £4,500. Cash inflows are £18,200 and cash outflows are £21,800. Calculate the closing balance.
practice_questions.marks:
Net cash flow = £18,200 − £21,800 = −£3,600.
Closing balance = £4,500 + (−£3,600) = £900.
1 mark for net cash flow correct.
2 marks for correct method shown for closing balance.
3 marks for correct final answer of £900 with £ sign.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a small bakery of a customer delaying payment on a £5,000 invoice by two months.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Sustained analysis across two linked impacts, applied to a small bakery, with clear chains of reasoning (e.g. £5,000 not received means the expected cash inflow is missed → closing balance is £5,000 lower → the bakery may struggle to pay suppliers and wages → it may need an overdraft which incurs interest, reducing profit).
Secure (3–4): Two relevant impacts with some application.
Developing (2): One impact explained; limited application.
Emerging (1): Basic point with no development.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: ‘The only way to solve a cash-flow problem is to take out an overdraft.’ Evaluate this statement. You should refer to at least one UK business in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments for the statement:
• Overdrafts are fast — useful when a shortfall is urgent.
• Flexible: interest is only paid on the amount used.
• Does not require collateral in the way a mortgage does.

Arguments against:
• Other solutions exist: re-schedule supplier payments, reduce outflows, chase invoices, increase inflows.
• Overdraft interest rates are high and the bank can demand repayment at any time.
• Dunelm and other retailers with seasonal sales manage with stock control and supplier credit, not just overdrafts.

Mastering (10–12): Sustained two-sided argument with applied UK context, clear chains of reasoning, and a justified conclusion (e.g. overdrafts are only one of four main tools and are best for short-term dips, not chronic shortfalls).
Secure (7–9): Balanced argument with some application and a conclusion.
Developing (4–6): Some argument; limited application or conclusion.
Emerging (1–3): Simple points with no real evaluation.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a financial method of motivation?
A) Fringe benefits
B) Greater responsibility
C) Commission
D) Democratic management style
practice_questions.marks:
C) Commission [1 mark]

Mastering: Correct answer selected.
Emerging: Incorrect answer.

practice_questions.text: Give two examples of fringe benefits a business could offer its staff.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (2 marks): Any two valid fringe benefits — company car, private healthcare, gym membership, free meals, childcare vouchers, staff discount, pension contribution, life insurance.
Secure (1 mark): One valid example.
Emerging (0 marks): Confuses fringe benefits with pay rises or commission.

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit to an estate agency of paying its sales staff on commission.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3 marks): Benefit identified (e.g. staff more motivated to complete sales) + ‘because’ clause (each sale directly increases personal income) + applied to estate agency (high-value transactions mean each extra sale boosts commission noticeably, driving effort).
Secure (2 marks): Benefit identified and explained but generic.
Developing (1 mark): Benefit named only.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant point.

practice_questions.text: A sales executive has a basic salary of £28,000 and earns 4% commission on total sales of £450,000. Calculate the executive’s total annual pay. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3 marks): Commission = 0.04 × £450,000 = £18,000. Total pay = £28,000 + £18,000 = £46,000. Working shown, unit (£) included.
Secure (2 marks): Correct commission (£18,000) but arithmetic slip in the total, or correct total with missing working.
Developing (1 mark): Some correct working (e.g. calculates 4% of 450,000).
Emerging (0 marks): No valid working.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a large supermarket of introducing a profit-sharing scheme for all staff.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Two developed chains of reasoning, e.g. staff feel ownership of results, which raises productivity and reduces till errors, which raises profit; however, in a year of low profit the bonus falls, which could demotivate staff and raise turnover just when the business can least afford it.
Secure (3–4 marks): One fully developed chain or two partial chains.
Developing (1–2 marks): Listed points with little development.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant analysis.

practice_questions.text: ‘For a call centre, paying higher wages is always the best way to motivate staff.’ Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): Balanced argument with developed points both sides — e.g. higher wages do cut turnover in a repetitive job market and attract candidates; but money alone cannot fix boring tasks, poor management or lack of progression, so non-financial methods (training, responsibility, supportive management) matter too. Judgement introduces a new weighting, e.g. ‘it depends on the local labour market — in low-unemployment areas, non-financial methods are decisive; in high-unemployment areas, wages can be enough’. Not a summary.
Secure (7–9 marks): Both sides present with some development, judgement offered.
Developing (4–6 marks): Mostly one-sided or listed points, limited evaluation.
Emerging (1–3 marks): Simple points, no evaluation.
No relevant content (0 marks).

practice_questions.text:
A bakery sells freshly baked bread at below cost to attract customers who then buy other items. Which pricing method is this?
A) Price skimming
B) Penetration pricing
C) Loss leader
D) Cost-plus
practice_questions.marks: C) Loss leader [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘unique selling point (USP)’.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for basic definition (e.g. what makes a product different).
2 marks for a clear, accurate definition (e.g. a feature that makes one product clearly different from its rivals and gives customers a reason to buy it).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why Apple uses price skimming when launching a new iPhone.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for identifying a valid reason (e.g. maximise early profits, cover R&D, position as premium).
2 marks for development (e.g. early adopters will pay a premium because the iPhone has new features no rival has yet).
3 marks for a developed point with consequence (e.g. … so Apple recovers its high research and development costs quickly, before rivals like Samsung copy the features and force prices down).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A manufacturer makes a product for £12 per unit and wants a 45% mark-up. Calculate the selling price using cost-plus pricing.
practice_questions.marks:
£12 × 1.45 = £17.40.
1 mark for correct method (mark-up calculation).
2 marks for correct working (12 + (12 × 0.45)).
3 marks for correct final answer of £17.40 with £ sign.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how having a strong brand image helps Nike maintain premium prices on its trainers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Sustained analysis with two linked points applied to Nike (e.g. brand image = performance + confidence → customers associate Nike with professional athletes → willing to pay more than for unbranded trainers → reduces price sensitivity; brand image also encourages repeat purchase → customer loyalty reduces need to compete on price).
Secure (3–4): Two relevant points identified with some application.
Developing (2): One point with limited application.
Emerging (1): Basic point with no application.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Aldi is considering launching a new premium own-brand chocolate range. Justify ONE pricing method they should use.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–9): Clear justified decision with sustained reasoning and comparison, applied to Aldi (e.g. competitive pricing — Aldi customers are price-sensitive, so pricing the premium range slightly below Cadbury or Lindt keeps Aldi’s value image while testing the premium market. Beats skimming which would clash with Aldi’s low-price brand, and beats cost-plus which ignores what rivals charge).
Secure (5–6): Method chosen with reasons, some comparison and application.
Developing (3–4): Method chosen with limited justification.
Emerging (1–2): Simple suggestion with no justification.
[9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a fixed cost for a bakery?
A) Flour
B) Packaging
C) The monthly rent on the shop
D) The electricity used by the oven each time bread is baked
practice_questions.marks: C) The monthly rent on the shop [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘variable cost’.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for a basic definition (e.g. ‘a cost that changes’).
2 marks for a clear, accurate definition (e.g. ‘a cost that changes directly with the level of output, such as raw materials or packaging’).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why rent is classed as a fixed cost rather than a variable cost.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for identifying that rent does not change with output.
2 marks for a developed point (e.g. the landlord charges the same sum every month regardless of how many units the business makes or sells).
3 marks for a fully developed point with a consequence (e.g. … which means the business still has to pay rent in a quiet month when sales are low, making fixed costs harder to cover).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A juice bar sells 600 smoothies in a week at £4 each. Fixed costs are £900 and variable costs are £1.50 per smoothie. Calculate the profit.

Revenue = 600 × £4 = £2,400.
Variable costs = 600 × £1.50 = £900.
Total costs = £900 + £900 = £1,800.
Profit = £2,400 − £1,800 = £600.
1 mark for correct revenue.
2 marks for correct total costs.
3 marks for correct final answer of £600 with £ sign.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a sudden rise in the price of raw materials would affect a UK chocolate manufacturer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Sustained analysis across two linked effects with chains of reasoning (e.g. cocoa and sugar are variable costs → a price rise increases variable cost per bar → so total costs rise while revenue stays the same → which squeezes profit margin → the manufacturer may pass the cost on through higher prices, risking lower sales, or absorb the cost and accept lower profit).
Secure (3–4): Two relevant effects explained with some application.
Developing (2): One effect explained; limited application.
Emerging (1): Basic point with no development.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: A UK cinema has high fixed costs but very low variable costs per viewer. A market trader selling sandwiches has low fixed costs but high variable costs per unit. Justify which of these two business models is less risky in a quiet month.
practice_questions.marks:
Cinema arguments:
• High fixed costs still have to be paid even if only a few tickets sell.
• Once fixed costs are covered, each extra ticket is near-pure profit.
• A quiet month can mean a large loss because fixed costs don’t flex.

Sandwich trader arguments:
• Low fixed costs mean little is owed when sales are low.
• Variable costs fall with sales, so total costs drop naturally.
• Lower profit per unit, but much lower downside risk.

Mastering (7–9): Clear recommendation (sandwich trader is less risky in a quiet month) with two developed reasons, weighed against the other option.
Secure (4–6): Recommendation with some reasoning on both sides.
Developing (2–3): One-sided argument, weak judgement.
Emerging (1): Simple preference only.
[9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is most likely if the Bank of England raises interest rates?
A) Borrowing becomes cheaper for businesses
B) Mortgage holders have more money to spend
C) Spending on luxury goods usually falls
D) Business investment in new machinery rises sharply
practice_questions.marks: C) Spending on luxury goods usually falls [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two ways in which a rise in interest rates can affect a small business.

One mark for any two of the following:
• Higher cost of loans or overdrafts / higher repayments [1 mark]
• Reduced consumer spending because customers have less disposable income [1 mark]
• Delayed investment in new equipment or premises [1 mark]
• Increased cost of hire purchase finance [1 mark]

Emerging: incorrect or confused.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way a rise in unemployment could affect a national supermarket chain.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• Identification: customers have less disposable income when more people are unemployed [1 mark].
• Development: they switch from premium supermarkets (Waitrose) to discount supermarkets (Aldi, Lidl) to cut their weekly shop [1 mark].
• Reasoning: so a national chain may see revenue shift between its stores, and should adjust product mix to include more value-tier ranges if it wants to keep market share [1 mark].

Mastering: identification, development AND a ‘because’ chain of reasoning.
Secure: identification and clear development.
Developing: correct identification with limited development.
Emerging: vague or incorrect point.
[3 marks]

Indicative working:

Emerging: incorrect approach.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse the likely impact of a rise in consumer spending on a UK high-street clothing retailer.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (accept developed reasoning that draws on one or more factors):
• Revenue: higher spending means customers buy more items per visit, which raises revenue.
• Margin: confidence lets the retailer hold prices or launch premium ranges, improving profit per sale.
• Investment: stronger cash flow supports opening new stores or refurbishing existing ones, which can lift future sales further.
• Competition: rivals also benefit, so success depends on keeping a clear point of difference (brand, service, style).
• Staffing: higher demand may mean hiring more staff — in a tight labour market this raises wage costs, partially offsetting the revenue gain.

Mastering: developed chains of reasoning using two or more factors, applied to a clothing retailer.
Secure: a developed chain on one factor plus a supporting point, applied.
Developing: relevant points listed with limited development or weak application.
Emerging: generic statements with no application.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘A rise in interest rates always hurts small UK businesses.’
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
Arguments in support:
• Loans, mortgages and overdrafts cost more, cutting profit for firms that are reliant on borrowing.
• Investment is delayed because fewer projects look worthwhile at higher borrowing costs.
• Customers spend less on non-essentials, so restaurants, cafés, boutiques and leisure firms see demand fall.
• Wage pressure may continue if employment stays high, further squeezing margins.

Arguments against:
• Businesses with cash savings earn more interest, boosting income rather than squeezing it.
• Firms that sell essentials (bread, milk, energy) see little change in demand.
• Discount retailers (Aldi, Lidl, Poundland) tend to gain market share as customers trade down.
• A rise in rates can strengthen the pound, lowering the cost of imported materials for firms that bring in supplies from abroad.

Conclusion should introduce a new weighting — for example, it depends on the type of business and how reliant it is on borrowing. The most important factor is the firm’s cost structure: heavily geared firms suffer, cash-rich firms may benefit.

Mastering: balanced argument with two developed points on each side and a justified conclusion that introduces a new weighting.
Secure: balanced argument with some development and a clear conclusion.
Developing: one-sided argument or conclusion that only summarises earlier points.
Emerging: brief points with no real evaluation or conclusion.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is the most likely main objective for a business in its first year of trading?
A) Maximising shareholder value
B) International expansion
C) Survival

In year one, covering costs and building a customer base matters more than large-scale targets.

practice_questions.text: Give two objectives that a public limited company (Plc) such as JD Sports might set itself.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per valid objective (max 2): profit maximisation, growth (domestic or international), market share, customer satisfaction, social/ethical objectives (e.g. sustainability), shareholder value. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: A business had total sales of £1,200,000. The total size of the market was £20,000,000. Calculate the business's market share. Give your answer as a percentage.
