Convert to percentage: 0.06 × 100 = 6 (1 mark).
Final answer with unit: 6% (1 mark).
Method marks awarded even if the final figure is wrong, provided the working is shown. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a business's objectives might change as it grows from a single-site start-up into a national chain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed chains of reasoning tracing how objectives shift, with named stages (e.g. survival → profit maximisation → growth → shareholder value/ethical) and clear cause-and-effect.
Secure: Two chains, at least one developed, relevant to a named business or realistic scenario.
Developing: Lists changes with limited explanation.
Emerging: States objectives without explaining the shift.
Indicative chains: (1) early on survival dominates because costs outstrip revenue → later, once cash flow stabilises, profit maximisation becomes possible → at national scale, growth and shareholder value take over because the business must justify itself to investors. (2) ethical/social objectives often emerge later because small firms cannot afford the extra cost → as scale brings profit, the business can invest in sustainability which also protects its brand. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: A growing bakery chain is choosing between (A) aggressive growth — opening 30 new stores in two years — or (B) focusing on customer satisfaction and slow, steady expansion. Justify which objective you would recommend.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear recommendation with two developed reasons (one fully explained), weighed against the rejected option, applied to a bakery chain, with explicit reference to risks and context (finance, competition, customer loyalty).
Secure: Clear recommendation, two developed reasons, some comparison.
Developing: Recommendation with reasons but limited weighting of the alternative.
Emerging: Lists advantages and disadvantages without a supported choice.
Indicative content for A: rapid market share gain locks competitors out; economies of scale drive down unit costs; but diseconomies of scale and cash-flow strain are real risks. For B: protects brand reputation, builds repeat custom, lower cash-flow risk; but rivals may grab market share first. Strong answers name the deciding factor (e.g. strength of competition, availability of finance) rather than defaulting to safety. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'The only objective that really matters for a business is maximising profit.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should give reasoned arguments for and against the statement and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments to support: profit funds investment and survival; without it a business eventually closes; shareholders expect a return; profit is the most objective measure of performance.
Arguments to challenge: a short-term profit focus can damage long-term performance (e.g. cutting quality reduces repeat custom); not-for-profits like Oxfam succeed without profit; ethical objectives build brand loyalty (Patagonia, Tony's Chocolonely); customer satisfaction often precedes profit; stakeholder conflict is worsened by pure profit focus; staff motivation can suffer.

Mastering: Balanced argument with developed points both sides, applied to named businesses, and a judgement introducing a new weighting (e.g. 'profit matters most in the short term for survival, but ethical and customer objectives protect profit in the long term').
Secure: Balanced argument with development both sides and a clear conclusion.
Developing: Some points either side, limited development.
Emerging: One-sided argument or generic list. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the best definition of Total Quality Management (TQM)?
A) Paying inspectors extra to catch faults at the end of the line
B) An approach where every employee is responsible for quality at every stage
C) Outsourcing all manufacturing to a specialist supplier
D) Recalling products once customers complain
practice_questions.marks: B) An approach where every employee is responsible for quality at every stage [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘product recall’.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (2): When a business asks customers to return an already-sold product because of a safety or quality defect — typically accompanied by a refund, repair or replacement.
Secure (1): Returning products because of a fault.
Emerging (0): Vague or incorrect — e.g. ‘when a shop takes products off the shelf’.

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit to a UK retailer such as John Lewis of maintaining high quality.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): A clear benefit with developed reasoning — e.g. High service quality builds customer loyalty (1), which means shoppers return to John Lewis even when rivals are cheaper (2), protecting revenue and allowing the retailer to charge a price premium that funds the training and after-sales support the brand is built on (3).
Secure (2): Benefit with some development.
Developing (1): Benefit identified without explanation.
Emerging (0): No valid benefit.

practice_questions.text: A bakery processes 5,000 loaves per week. In an average week, 120 loaves are rejected at quality inspection. Calculate the defect rate as a percentage, to one decimal place.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): Defect rate = (120 ÷ 5,000) × 100 (1) = 2.4% (2). Correct percentage with working and units (3).
Secure (2): Correct method but arithmetic slip or missing percentage sign.
Developing (1): Shows ratio 120/5,000 without converting.
Emerging (0): No valid method. Method marks are awarded even if the final figure is wrong, so working must be shown.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a growing UK franchise such as Greggs of introducing Total Quality Management across all stores.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): A developed chain of reasoning drawing on more than one factor. E.g. TQM would train every store team to spot quality issues in food, service and cleanliness, so defects are caught before they reach customers. This reduces wasted stock and speeds up service, cutting costs and improving the customer experience. Stronger reputation supports price rises and new store openings. However, TQM demands heavy training investment and ongoing audits, which push up short-run costs and can be resisted by franchisees who resent head-office control. The net effect is likely positive long term but disruptive during rollout.
Secure (3–4): Clear analysis of at least one impact with some development.
Developing (1–2): Identifies effects without developing reasoning.
Emerging (0): No valid impact.

practice_questions.text: ‘Maintaining high quality always leads to higher profits.’ Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Higher quality builds brand reputation, supports a price premium and drives repeat purchases — John Lewis’s service model lets it charge more than discount retailers on similar goods.
• TQM reduces defects, returns and recalls, cutting the waste and rework bill.
• Strong online reviews lift conversion and reduce customer-acquisition costs.

Arguments against:
• Higher quality has real costs — staff training, inspection equipment, better materials — which can squeeze short-run margins, especially for a small business.
• In price-sensitive markets (budget supermarkets, pound shops) customers buy on price; paying for extra quality produces little extra revenue.
• A business can invest in quality and still lose money if demand collapses for reasons unrelated to quality, such as a recession or disruptive new competitor.

Judgement (Mastering 10–12): Quality lifts profits only if the market values it. For premium brands and loyalty-driven businesses, quality is one of the strongest profit drivers. For commodity sellers competing on price, over-investment in quality can erode profit — the conclusion must introduce a weighting (‘it depends on the market’) rather than summarise points already made.
Secure (7–9): Balanced points both sides with a clear judgement, some development.
Developing (4–6): Lists points each side without a real judgement.
Emerging (1–3): One-sided or underdeveloped.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a stakeholder group that would MOST directly oppose a decision to open a 24-hour warehouse next to a housing estate?
A) Shareholders
B) Customers
C) The local community
D) Suppliers
practice_questions.marks:
C) The local community [1 mark]
Noise, traffic and pollution at night directly affect residents living nearby.

practice_questions.text: Give two objectives that suppliers of a business usually have.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per valid objective (max 2): prompt payment, repeat orders, long-term contracts, fair prices, clear communication about changing demand. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why employees could be considered the most important stakeholder group for a small family restaurant.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: identifies a reason (skilled staff affect quality; staff represent the brand to customers; low turnover saves recruitment costs; staff motivation drives customer service).
2 marks: a 'because' clause explains the reason.
3 marks: links to the specific family restaurant context.
Indicative answer: 'Employees directly shape the customer experience (1) because diners remember the quality of service, food presentation and friendliness more than the restaurant's advertising (2), so for a family restaurant relying on repeat custom, staff are the single biggest driver of success (3).' [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a decision by a large supermarket to switch to self-service checkouts could affect two of its stakeholder groups.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two groups chosen, each developed into a full chain of reasoning (stakeholder → consequence → business impact), with clear cause-effect logic.
Secure: Two groups with at least one fully developed chain.
Developing: Two groups named with partial development.
Emerging: Lists groups without explaining impact.
Indicative chains: (1) Employees — fewer cashiers needed → redundancies or redeployment → lower morale, possible strike action → disruption to store operations. (2) Customers — faster queues for small baskets → convenience for regulars, but older or less digitally confident customers feel excluded → lost sales to rival supermarkets with staffed tills. (3) Shareholders — lower wage bill → higher profit margins → rising dividend. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: A clothing retailer is deciding whether to (A) raise prices to fund a 10% pay rise for warehouse staff or (B) keep prices flat and pay a larger dividend to shareholders. Justify which option you would recommend.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear recommendation with two developed reasons (one fully explained), weighed against the rejected option, applied to a retailer with explicit reference to stakeholder impact and brand reputation.
Secure: Clear recommendation, two developed reasons, some comparison.
Developing: Recommendation with reasons but limited weighting.
Emerging: Lists impacts without a supported recommendation.
Indicative content for A: improves staff retention and productivity, protects brand reputation after fast-fashion pay scandals (e.g. Boohoo), appeals to ethical consumers; but risks losing price-sensitive customers in a tough market. For B: rewards owners, signals a strong financial performance to investors, supports share price; but risks strike action, media backlash and reputational damage. A strong answer names whether long-term brand protection or short-term shareholder return should drive the decision. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Shareholders should always come first when a business makes a decision.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should give reasoned arguments to support and challenge the statement and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments to support: shareholders own the business and fund its operations; without their capital the business could not exist; dividends and share price are the reward for risk; Plcs are legally answerable to shareholders; aligned incentives drive efficiency.
Arguments to challenge: ignoring staff causes strikes, recruitment costs and reputational damage (e.g. Amazon warehouse disputes); unhappy customers switch to rivals; supplier relationships break down; community opposition can block planning; ethical brands (Patagonia, Tony's Chocolonely) thrive precisely by putting people or planet before pure shareholder returns; long-term shareholder value is damaged by short-term-only thinking.

Mastering: Balanced argument with developed points both sides, applied to named businesses, and a judgement introducing a new weighting (e.g. 'depends on the ownership structure and time horizon').
Secure: Balanced argument with development both sides and clear conclusion.
Developing: Some points either side with limited development.
Emerging: One-sided argument without evaluation. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of off-the-job training?
A) A new waiter watching a senior colleague take an order
B) A barista practising on the coffee machine during a quiet shift
C) An apprentice attending college one day a week
D) A new employee being shown the fire exits on their first day
practice_questions.marks:
C) An apprentice attending college one day a week [1 mark]

Mastering: Correct answer selected.
Emerging: Incorrect answer.

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘induction training’.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (2 marks): Clear definition — training given to new employees when they start, covering the business, their role and essential procedures.
Secure (1 mark): Basic idea (e.g. ‘training for new employees’) without precise detail.
Emerging (0 marks): Confuses induction with general training or with on-the-job training.

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit to a Premier League academy of using on-the-job training for young coaches.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3 marks): Benefit identified (e.g. skills learned are directly relevant) + ‘because’ clause (new coaches practise on the same pitches and players they will manage) + applied to academy (means coaching style stays consistent with the club’s philosophy).
Secure (2 marks): Benefit identified and explained but generic.
Developing (1 mark): Benefit named only.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant point.

practice_questions.text: A business sends 8 employees on an off-the-job training course. The course costs £450 per employee and each employee loses 2 days of output worth £160 per day. Calculate the total cost to the business of the training. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3 marks): Course cost = 8 × £450 = £3,600. Lost output = 8 × 2 × £160 = £2,560. Total = £6,160. Working shown, unit (£) included.
Secure (2 marks): One subtotal correct but error in the other, or correct total without working.
Developing (1 mark): Some correct working (e.g. spots 8 × £450).
Emerging (0 marks): No valid working.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a large supermarket of the introduction of self-service checkouts and the training needed to support them.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Two developed chains of reasoning, e.g. retraining staff to help customers with self-checkouts speeds up queues and raises customer service, which boosts loyalty; however, training time is expensive and older staff may resist the change, leading to short-term productivity losses before gains appear.
Secure (3–4 marks): One fully developed chain or two partial chains.
Developing (1–2 marks): Listed points with little development.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant analysis.

practice_questions.text: A growing bakery with 20 staff needs to train new assistants. The owner is choosing between on-the-job training led by existing bakers, or sending new assistants on a one-week off-the-job course at a local college. Justify which method the owner should choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–9 marks): Two developed reasons for the chosen option (one fully explained) — e.g. on-the-job is cheaper for a small bakery, keeps staff available to serve customers, and trainees learn the house recipes exactly. Weighed against counter (college course offers food-hygiene qualification, reduces the load on senior bakers). Clear judgement matched to the specific bakery.
Secure (4–6 marks): Some development of both options. Judgement present but brief.
Developing (1–3 marks): Mainly listing pros and cons.
Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content.

practice_questions.text:
Which stage of the product life cycle sees sales rising most rapidly?
A) Introduction
B) Growth
C) Maturity
D) Decline
practice_questions.marks: B) Growth [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two extension strategies a business could use to delay the decline of a product.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark per correct strategy, up to 2.
Accept any two of: updating packaging, adding more or different features, changing target market, advertising, price reduction.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why a business would classify Cadbury Dairy Milk as a ‘cash cow’ on the Boston Matrix.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for identifying cash cow features (low market growth, high market share).
2 marks for development (e.g. the UK chocolate market is mature and slow-growing but Dairy Milk has the highest share).
3 marks for a developed point with consequence (e.g. … so Dairy Milk generates steady profit for Mondelez which can be used to fund newer products that are still Question Marks or Stars).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A product has UK sales of £84 million in a market worth £420 million. Calculate the product’s market share.
practice_questions.marks:
Market share = (84 ÷ 420) × 100 = 20%.
1 mark for correct formula.
2 marks for correct substitution and working.
3 marks for correct final answer of 20% with % sign.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the Boston Matrix could help a large food manufacturer manage its product portfolio.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Sustained analysis with two linked benefits, clear chains of reasoning, and application to a named food manufacturer (e.g. Mondelez or Nestlé). E.g. classifying each product reveals which earn cash (Cash Cows) and which drain it (Question Marks) → directs investment to Stars and newly promising Question Marks → balances portfolio so declining products are replaced by rising ones → protects long-term revenue.
Secure (3–4): Two benefits identified; some application.
Developing (2): One benefit; limited application.
Emerging (1): Basic point with no application.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: ‘Using extension strategies is always better than launching a new product.’ Evaluate this statement. Refer to at least one named UK business in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments for:
• Extension is cheaper than R&D — Cadbury extends Dairy Milk constantly without designing a brand-new bar.
• Uses existing brand loyalty — customers already trust the product, reducing launch risk.
• Keeps revenue flowing from a Cash Cow while management plans the next Star.

Arguments against:
• Extension only delays decline — Nokia’s feature-phone extensions did not save it from the smartphone shift.
• Fast-moving markets (tech, fashion) reward brand-new products — Apple’s whole-new categories (iPhone, AirPods) drove huge growth.
• Extension can confuse the brand if it goes too far (too many flavours, packaging changes).
• Skipping new product launches risks being left behind by rivals who do innovate.

Mastering (10–12): Sustained two-sided argument with named UK businesses, clear chains of reasoning and a justified conclusion (e.g. ‘depends on the stage of the product and the market’).
Secure (7–9): Balanced argument with some application and a conclusion.
Developing (4–6): Some argument on one or both sides; limited application.
Emerging (1–3): Simple points with no real evaluation.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is most likely if the pound strengthens against the US dollar?
A) UK exports become cheaper for American buyers
B) UK exports become more expensive for American buyers
C) UK firms importing materials from the US pay more
D) UK holidaymakers in the US find everything more expensive
practice_questions.marks: B) UK exports become more expensive for American buyers [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘globalisation’.
practice_questions.marks:
The process by which businesses, economies and cultures around the world become more connected [1 mark] and trade more freely across national borders [1 mark].

Mastering: precise definition using correct business vocabulary.
Secure: accurate meaning with an example.
Developing: partial meaning or vague.
Emerging: definition incorrect or confused.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way a UK manufacturer that imports raw materials from the EU could be affected by a fall in the value of the pound.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• Identification: a fall in the pound means it takes more pounds to buy the same amount of euros [1 mark].
• Development: so the cost of imported raw materials rises for the UK manufacturer [1 mark].
• Reasoning: because costs are higher, profit margins are squeezed, and the firm may need to raise prices or absorb the cost, which could reduce competitiveness [1 mark].

Mastering: identification, development AND a ‘because’ chain of reasoning.
Secure: identification and clear development.
Developing: correct identification with limited development.
Emerging: vague or incorrect point.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a UK whisky distiller of an increase in overseas demand for its products.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (accept developed reasoning that draws on one or more factors):
• Revenue: higher export sales directly raise revenue, especially valuable given the UK market is mature.
• Unit costs: higher volumes allow economies of scale, reducing cost per bottle and raising margins.
• Investment: extra profit supports reinvestment in new stills, warehousing and marketing abroad.
• Exchange-rate risk: earnings in dollars or euros are exposed to currency swings — a stronger pound later would cut the sterling value of overseas sales.
• Supply risk: the distiller needs to scale up safely or it could lose quality, damaging the premium reputation that drove demand in the first place.

Mastering: developed chains of reasoning using two or more factors, applied to the distiller.
Secure: a developed chain on one factor plus a supporting point, applied.
Developing: relevant points listed with limited development or weak application.
Emerging: generic statements with no application.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A UK cycling-kit manufacturer is deciding how to respond to rising international demand:
Option 1 — Open a small sales office in the United States with local staff.
Option 2 — Expand an e-commerce platform in multiple languages from the UK.
Justify which option the manufacturer should choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
Option 1 (sales office):
• Builds local knowledge and customer relationships in a huge market.
• Physical presence can help with returns and customer service.
• Drawback: expensive — office rent, staff wages in dollars, visas; slow to set up.
Option 2 (e-commerce):
• Lower set-up cost and faster to launch; reaches many countries at once.
• Uses data from existing UK site to target marketing abroad.
• Drawback: no physical presence; returns and customer service costs rise as overseas sales grow; exchange-rate risk cuts through to the bottom line.

Justification must pick one option and weigh it against the other. A strong answer might argue that e-commerce is better for a small firm because it spreads risk across many markets with lower capital outlay. A different strong answer might argue the sales office suits a firm with premium products where local presence builds trust.

Mastering: clear decision with two developed reasons, weighed against the rejected option, applied.
Secure: decision with one developed reason, supporting point, and some weighing.
Developing: decision stated with limited reasoning or weak weighing.
Emerging: lists pros and cons of both options with no clear decision.
[9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘Globalisation is more of a threat than an opportunity for small UK businesses.’
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
Arguments in support (threat):
• Small UK firms face tough competition from overseas producers with much lower labour and material costs.
• Supply-chain shocks (Suez Canal, pandemic chip shortages, tariffs) hit small firms hardest because they lack the scale to absorb disruption.
• Exchange-rate swings make costs and revenues unpredictable, and small firms cannot easily hedge.

Arguments against (opportunity):
• E-commerce tools (Shopify, Amazon, Etsy) open global export markets that used to need a sales team in each country.
• Access to cheap overseas suppliers lowers costs for small manufacturers.
• Global platforms (Instagram, TikTok) provide low-cost marketing to customers worldwide.
• A weak pound can make UK exports more competitive abroad, boosting small exporter revenue.

Conclusion should introduce a new weighting — for example, it depends on the type of product and how digitally ready the firm is. The most important factor is probably whether the firm can differentiate on quality, design or niche rather than price.

Mastering: balanced argument with two developed points on each side and a justified conclusion that introduces a new weighting.
Secure: balanced argument with some development and a clear conclusion.
Developing: one-sided argument or conclusion that only summarises earlier points.
Emerging: brief points with no real evaluation or conclusion.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes ‘margin of safety’?
A) The profit made on each unit sold
B) The difference between actual sales and the break-even point
C) The total fixed costs of the business
D) The percentage return on an investment
practice_questions.marks: B) The difference between actual sales and the break-even point [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘break-even’.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for a basic definition (e.g. ‘where costs equal revenue’).
2 marks for a clear, accurate definition (e.g. ‘the level of output where total revenue equals total costs, so the business makes neither profit nor loss’).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one limitation of using ARR to judge an investment project.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for identifying a valid limitation (e.g. ignores timing of cash flows, ignores risk, based on forecasts that may be wrong).
2 marks for a developed point (e.g. ARR treats £1,000 profit in year 1 the same as £1,000 profit in year 5, even though money now is worth more than money later).
3 marks for a fully developed point with a consequence (e.g. … so the business may pick a project with high long-term profit over one with quicker, more certain returns, tying up cash for longer than needed).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A bakery sells loaves for £2.50 each. Variable cost per loaf is £0.90. Weekly fixed costs are £800. Calculate the break-even point in units.
practice_questions.marks:
Contribution per loaf = £2.50 − £0.90 = £1.60.
Break-even = £800 ÷ £1.60 = 500 loaves per week.
1 mark for correct contribution.
2 marks for correct method (fixed costs ÷ contribution).
3 marks for correct final answer of 500 loaves.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A business invests £50,000 in new machinery. Over 4 years the machinery generates a total profit of £24,000. Calculate the average rate of return (ARR).
practice_questions.marks:
Average annual profit = £24,000 ÷ 4 = £6,000.
ARR = (£6,000 ÷ £50,000) × 100 = 12%.
1 mark for correct average annual profit.
2 marks for correct method shown.
3 marks for correct final answer of 12% with % sign.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how a rise in fixed costs would affect the break-even point and margin of safety of a UK coffee shop.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Sustained analysis across both break-even and margin of safety with clear chains of reasoning (e.g. higher fixed costs → fixed costs ÷ contribution gives a larger number → break-even point rises → if actual sales stay the same, the gap between actual sales and break-even shrinks → margin of safety falls → the shop is now more vulnerable to a small drop in sales).
Secure (3–4): Two effects explained with some application.
Developing (2): One effect explained; limited application.
Emerging (1): Basic point with no development.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the best example of a post-sales service?
A) An advert on Instagram promoting a new product
B) A store layout designed to feel welcoming
C) A five-year warranty and a help line for troubleshooting a new washing machine
D) A shop mannequin dressed in the latest range
practice_questions.marks: C) A five-year warranty and a help line for troubleshooting a new washing machine [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘customer loyalty’.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (2): The tendency of a customer to continue buying from the same business repeatedly rather than switching to a competitor, usually built on trust, satisfaction and positive past experience.
Secure (1): Customers returning to buy from the same business.
Emerging (0): Vague or incorrect — e.g. ‘when a business has lots of customers’.

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit to John Lewis of training its partners to have strong product knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): A clear benefit with a developed chain — e.g. Strong product knowledge lets partners match shoppers to the right appliance (1), which means customers leave satisfied and are more likely to return rather than switch to a cheaper rival (2), lifting repeat revenue and supporting the price premium John Lewis charges (3).
Secure (2): Benefit stated with some development.
Developing (1): Benefit identified without explanation.
Emerging (0): No valid benefit.

practice_questions.text: Last year a retailer had 20,000 customer orders; 14,400 customers returned to place a further order. Calculate the customer-retention rate as a percentage.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (3): Retention rate = (14,400 ÷ 20,000) × 100 (1) = 72% (2). Correct answer with percentage sign and working (3).
Secure (2): Correct method but arithmetic slip or missing percentage sign.
Developing (1): Ratio 14,400/20,000 shown without converting.
Emerging (0): No valid method. Method marks are awarded even if the final figure is wrong, so working must be shown.

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a broadband provider of social-media complaints from dissatisfied customers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): A developed chain of reasoning drawing on more than one factor. E.g. Complaints on X or Facebook are seen by thousands of potential customers, so poor service damages reputation far beyond the individual case. This pushes switchers to rivals when contracts expire, reducing revenue. However, social media also gives the provider a chance to respond publicly — a fast, helpful reply in the same thread can turn the complaint into a marketing moment. The net impact depends on how quickly and skilfully the provider handles the thread; mishandling amplifies the damage, good handling can actually build trust.
Secure (3–4): Clear analysis of at least one impact with some development.
Developing (1–2): Identifies effects without developing reasoning.
Emerging (0): No valid impact.

practice_questions.text: Marcus runs a small electronics shop and is deciding whether to invest £4,000 in a staff-training programme focused on product knowledge and after-sales support. Justify whether he should make this investment.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (8–9): A clear decision supported by two developed reasons weighed against the alternative, applied to Marcus’s context. E.g. Marcus should invest. Electronics customers are often uncertain about which product to buy, so trained staff translate that uncertainty into a sale and into confidence that after-sales help will be available if needed. Repeat custom and word-of-mouth are worth far more than £4,000 over a year, especially in a small shop that cannot compete on price with national chains. The alternative — not training — saves the fee but risks losing customers to better-informed rivals, a much bigger long-run cost.
Secure (5–7): A clear judgement with two reasons but uneven development or limited handling of the alternative.
Developing (3–4): Reasons listed each side without a committed judgement.
Emerging (1–2): Describes the options without choosing.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of employment law?
A) A requirement that goods match their description
B) A legal minimum hourly wage
C) A law requiring a clear fire exit
D) A rule that advertisements cannot mislead customers
practice_questions.marks: B) A legal minimum hourly wage [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two ways in which consumer law protects customers when they buy products from a UK business.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for any two of the following:
• Goods must match the description given by the seller [1 mark]
• Goods must be of satisfactory quality [1 mark]
• Goods must be fit for their intended purpose [1 mark]
• Customers have a right to refunds, repairs or replacements for faulty goods [1 mark]
• Adverts must not be misleading (trade descriptions) [1 mark]

Mastering: two precise, separate protections using correct business vocabulary.
Secure: two correct protections.
Developing: one correct protection; second vague or repeated.
Emerging: incorrect or confused.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one way a rise in the National Minimum Wage could affect a small restaurant.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
• Identification: the restaurant’s wage bill rises because it must pay every eligible employee more per hour [1 mark].
• Development: this cuts the profit margin on every meal served unless prices are raised [1 mark].
• Reasoning: so the owner may have to increase menu prices, which could reduce demand, or cut back on staff hours, which could affect service quality and customer satisfaction [1 mark].

Mastering: identification, development AND a ‘because’ chain of reasoning.
Secure: identification and clear development.
Developing: correct identification with limited development.
Emerging: vague or incorrect point.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse the impact on a UK supermarket of increased competition from a new discount rival opening nearby.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content (accept developed reasoning that draws on one or more factors):
• Price: the supermarket may cut prices on key lines to protect market share, which squeezes profit margin.
• Product: it may expand its own-brand value range to match the discounter, taking shelf space from premium lines.
• Promotion: more spending on loyalty schemes (Clubcard, Nectar) to lock in existing customers.
• Service: improved in-store experience (cleaner stores, longer opening hours, faster checkouts) to offer something the discounter does not.
• Risk: if it cannot match the discounter on price, it risks losing customers who trade down, especially during a cost-of-living squeeze.

Mastering: developed chains of reasoning using two or more factors, applied to the supermarket.
Secure: a developed chain on one factor plus a supporting point, applied.
Developing: relevant points listed with limited development or weak application.
Emerging: generic statements with no application.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A UK builder is deciding how to respond to a tightening of health and safety enforcement on construction sites:
Option 1 — Invest in new safety equipment and full training for all site staff.
Option 2 — Hire a specialist health-and-safety consultant to review and improve procedures without buying new equipment.
Justify which option the builder should choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
Option 1 (equipment and training):
• Directly reduces accident risk on site — protects workers and the business’s reputation.
• Training means every worker is aware of updated rules, reducing liability.
• Drawback: significant upfront cost; new equipment may be underused if practices do not change.
Option 2 (consultant):
• Cheaper in the short term — no large equipment bill.
• A specialist brings wider industry experience and can redesign procedures.
• Drawback: advice is only as good as the implementation; without investment in equipment some hazards remain.

Justification must choose one option and weigh it against the other. A strong answer might argue that equipment plus training is worth the investment because accidents on construction sites can kill and fines are huge, so prevention is cheaper than cure. A different strong answer might argue the consultant-first approach is sensible because it identifies priorities before spending money.

Mastering: clear decision with two developed reasons, weighed against the rejected option, applied.
Secure: decision with one developed reason, supporting point, and some weighing.
Developing: decision stated with limited reasoning or weak weighing.
Emerging: lists pros and cons of both options with no clear decision.
[9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
‘The more laws that apply to a business, the harder it is to make a profit.’
Evaluate this statement.
practice_questions.marks:
Indicative content:
Arguments in support:
• Employment laws raise wage bills through the minimum wage, pensions auto-enrolment and holiday pay.
• Health and safety compliance requires training, equipment, risk assessments and record keeping — all costly.
• Consumer law means refunds, recalls and restrictions on advertising, adding cost and limiting marketing.
• Small firms carry the relative burden most heavily because compliance costs are similar but revenues are smaller.

Arguments against:
• Laws create a level playing field — rivals cannot cut corners to undercut compliant firms.
• Compliant businesses avoid fines, lawsuits and brand-damaging scandals (e.g. the supplier-wage scandals at Boohoo).
• Better-treated staff are more motivated, reducing turnover and training costs — which supports profit.
• Safer workplaces mean fewer accidents, lower insurance, and less lost production.
• Laws can attract ethical customers and staff, building reputation.

Conclusion should introduce a new weighting — for example, it depends on the size and type of business. For a small new firm, compliance cost may be a heavy burden in year one; for an established firm, the costs are usually outweighed by reputational gain and risk reduction. The most important factor is how well the business plans for compliance before it becomes a problem.

Mastering: balanced argument with two developed points on each side and a justified conclusion that introduces a new weighting.
Secure: balanced argument with some development and a clear conclusion.
Developing: one-sided argument or conclusion that only summarises earlier points.
Emerging: brief points with no real evaluation or conclusion.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an asset?
A) A bank loan
B) Unpaid invoices from suppliers
C) A delivery van owned by the business
D) A mortgage on the premises
practice_questions.marks: C) A delivery van owned by the business [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘gross profit’.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for a basic definition (e.g. ‘revenue minus costs’).
2 marks for a clear, accurate definition (e.g. ‘revenue minus the cost of sales — the profit made on the products themselves before running costs are deducted’).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why a business might have a high gross profit margin but a low net profit margin.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for identifying that running costs (rent, marketing, salaries) are eating into profit.
2 marks for a developed point (e.g. the business makes good money on each product sold but spends heavily on overheads like rent and marketing).
3 marks for a fully developed point with a consequence (e.g. … which means although individual products are profitable, the business keeps only a small fraction of revenue as net profit and may need to cut overheads or raise prices to improve).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A business has revenue of £250,000, cost of sales of £150,000 and other operating costs of £75,000. Calculate the gross profit margin.
practice_questions.marks:
Gross profit = £250,000 − £150,000 = £100,000.
Gross profit margin = (£100,000 ÷ £250,000) × 100 = 40%.
1 mark for correct gross profit.
2 marks for correct method shown.
3 marks for correct final answer of 40% with % sign.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A UK bakery has a net profit margin of 6% this year, compared to 10% last year. Analyse two possible reasons for this fall in net profit margin.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Sustained analysis of two linked reasons with chains of reasoning (e.g. supplier costs rose → cost of sales increased → gross profit margin shrank → less money left over to cover overheads → net profit margin fell; AND overheads rose e.g. rent went up → fixed costs grew → net profit margin fell even though revenue was stable).
Secure (3–4): Two reasons explained with some application.
Developing (2): One reason explained; limited application.
Emerging (1): Basic point with no development.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: ‘A business with a rising gross profit margin is always performing well.’ Evaluate this statement. You should refer to at least one UK business in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments for the statement:
• A rising gross profit margin shows the business is either raising prices successfully or cutting the cost of each unit — both suggest strong buying power or premium positioning.
• More gross profit means more money available to cover overheads and generate net profit.
• Premium retailers like Burberry demonstrate this — high gross margins support the brand model.

Arguments against:
• A rising gross profit margin tells you nothing about overheads. If rent, marketing and admin costs rise faster, net profit margin can still fall.
• Gross profit margin ignores cash flow — a business can be profitable on paper and still fail if it can’t pay bills (see cash-flow lesson).
• Context matters — a supermarket like Tesco operates on a gross margin around 7% by design; comparing it to Burberry’s 70% is meaningless.

Mastering (10–12): Sustained two-sided argument with UK business application, chains of reasoning, and a justified conclusion (e.g. gross profit margin is one indicator, but judgement requires context and multiple metrics).
Secure (7–9): Balanced argument with some application and conclusion.
Developing (4–6): Some argument; limited application or conclusion.
Emerging (1–3): Simple points with no real evaluation.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which location factor is MOST important for a new independent coffee shop opening in a town centre?
A) Proximity to raw materials
B) Proximity to the market (customers)
C) Proximity to government offices
D) Proximity to a university library
practice_questions.marks:
B) Proximity to the market (customers) [1 mark]
A coffee shop depends on passing foot traffic — without customers within walking distance it will fail regardless of other factors.

practice_questions.text: Give two costs that are likely to differ between locating a warehouse in central London and locating one in Doncaster.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark per valid difference (max 2): rent / business rates, wages (higher in London), transport / delivery costs to London markets, utilities, congestion charges. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: A retailer pays £480,000 in annual rent at its current site. A new site costs £300,000 per year. Calculate the percentage saving the retailer would make on rent by moving. Give your answer to one decimal place.
practice_questions.marks:
Working: saving = £480,000 − £300,000 = £180,000 (1 mark).
Percentage saving = 180,000 ÷ 480,000 × 100 (1 mark for correct method).
= 37.5% (1 mark for final answer with unit).
Method marks awarded for showing working even if final number is slightly off. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse the factors a fish and chip restaurant might consider when choosing where to locate in a small UK seaside town.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or more factors developed with clear chains of reasoning tying the factor to a specific effect on the restaurant (e.g. proximity to market → near the seafront car park and promenade → high summer footfall → higher revenue).
Secure: Two factors explained with relevant cause-and-effect links, applied to a seaside context.
Developing: Lists factors with partial explanation.
Emerging: Names factors without explaining their impact.
Indicative content: proximity to market (seafront footfall), raw materials (local fish supplies, cost of transport if inland), labour (seasonal staff availability), competition (too close to rivals = split trade), costs (beachfront rent vs back-street rent). A developed answer identifies the trade-off: high seafront rent vs high footfall. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: An online clothing start-up is choosing between (A) leasing a warehouse unit in central Manchester close to its staff or (B) leasing a larger unit 40 miles outside Manchester near the M6 motorway. Justify which option you would recommend.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear recommendation with two developed reasons (one fully explained), weighed against the rejected option, applied to an online clothing retailer with reference to specific factors (transport, labour, rent, delivery speed).
Secure: Clear recommendation, two developed reasons, some comparison.
Developing: Recommendation with reasons but limited evaluation.
Emerging: Lists pros and cons without a supported choice.
Indicative content for A: easier to attract and retain staff, shorter commute = better morale, proximity to city suppliers and returns processing; higher rent and business rates, congestion slows delivery vans. For B: cheaper rent means more space for stock, direct motorway access speeds next-day delivery, easier to scale; but recruiting and retaining staff harder, commute costs may deter applicants. A strong answer names the deciding factor — delivery speed or staff retention — and links it back to the start-up's growth stage. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'Cost is always the most important factor when choosing a business location.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should give reasoned arguments for and against the statement and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments to support: cost directly affects profit margins and break-even; high rent or wages can sink a small business (e.g. high-street closures after rent rises); cheap locations free up cash for investment; government grants and cheap regions (e.g. Enterprise Zones) deliberately use cost to attract firms.
Arguments to challenge: a cheap site with no customers has no revenue; luxury brands need prestige addresses (Bond Street jewellers); manufacturers must be near raw materials; service businesses need footfall; skilled labour may only exist in expensive regions (tech in Cambridge, finance in London); long-term brand damage from a poor address can cost more than the rent saved.

Mastering: Balanced argument with developed points both sides, applied to real businesses, and a judgement that introduces a new weighting (e.g. 'cost matters most for firms competing on low prices; prestige or access matters most for firms competing on experience').
Secure: Balanced argument with development both sides and clear conclusion.
Developing: Some points either side, limited development.
Emerging: One-sided argument without evaluation. [12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A business runs a ‘buy one, get one free’ offer in its supermarket for two weeks. Which type of promotion is this?
A) PR
B) Advertising
C) Sales promotion
D) Sponsorship
practice_questions.marks: C) Sales promotion [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Give two examples of sales promotion methods listed in the specification.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark per correct method, up to 2.
Accept any two of: point-of-sale displays, 2-for-1 offers, free gifts, samples, coupons, competitions.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit to Gymshark of using social media influencers to promote its clothing.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for identifying a benefit (e.g. reaches target market, cheaper than TV, trusted by followers).
2 marks for development (e.g. fitness influencers on Instagram have large followings of gym-goers aged 18–30 — Gymshark’s exact target segment).
3 marks for a developed point with consequence (e.g. … so marketing spend reaches the right customers directly and influencer endorsements feel authentic, driving higher conversion than paid TV adverts aimed at a general audience).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A business has a £24,000 promotion budget. It spends 30% on social media and the rest on TV adverts. Calculate how much is spent on TV adverts.
practice_questions.marks:
£24,000 × 0.70 = £16,800 (or £24,000 − £7,200).
1 mark for correct method (70% or subtract 30%).
2 marks for correct working.
3 marks for correct final answer of £16,800 with £ sign.
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how Cadbury uses TV advertising at Christmas to increase sales of its chocolate products.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Sustained analysis applied to Cadbury with clear chains of reasoning (e.g. Christmas TV adverts reach mass family audiences watching shows like Strictly → build emotional image linking Cadbury to family and tradition → shoppers buy Dairy Milk tins as gifts → increases December sales and protects Dairy Milk’s Cash Cow position). Answer references image, sales and reach.
Secure (3–4): Two points identified with some application.
Developing (2): One point with limited application.
Emerging (1): Basic generic point with no named business.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: A new independent UK coffee shop is deciding how to promote itself. Justify ONE promotional method they should use.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–9): Clear justified decision with sustained reasoning and comparison (e.g. social media — low cost suits a start-up’s small budget, reaches local customers, easy to update with daily specials, beats TV advertising which is unaffordable and too broadly targeted). Includes application to the coffee shop context.
Secure (5–6): Method chosen with reasoning and some comparison.
Developing (3–4): Method chosen with limited justification.
Emerging (1–2): Simple suggestion with no comparison.
[9 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the best example of a pure e-commerce UK retailer?
A) Primark
B) ASOS
C) John Lewis department stores
D) Greggs
practice_questions.marks: B) ASOS [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term ‘m-commerce’.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for a basic definition (e.g. selling through mobile phones).
2 marks for a clear, accurate definition (e.g. buying and selling products and services through mobile devices, typically via apps or mobile-optimised websites).
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit to ASOS of using e-commerce rather than high-street shops.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for identifying a benefit (e.g. reach, 24/7 trading, lower rent, global markets, data collection).
2 marks for development (e.g. ASOS has no high-street rent or shop staff costs, just warehouses and website).
3 marks for a developed point with consequence (e.g. … so ASOS’s lower overheads let it offer competitive prices to its fashion-conscious target market while still making a profit, something Debenhams could not match with its expensive shop estate).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: A UK fashion retailer sells 60,000 items a month, of which 75% are sold online. Calculate how many items are sold online each month.
practice_questions.marks:
60,000 × 0.75 = 45,000 items.
1 mark for correct method (multiply by 0.75 or 75%).
2 marks for correct working.
3 marks for correct final answer of 45,000 (accept ‘items’).
[3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how the four Ps of the marketing mix work together for Primark to create a clear customer message.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6): Sustained analysis of at least three Ps working together for Primark (e.g. product — fashionable basics; price — low; promotion — almost none, word-of-mouth; place — big flagship stores on main high streets, click-and-collect only, no home delivery). All reinforce the same ‘cheap fast fashion’ image.
Secure (3–4): Two Ps discussed with some application.
Developing (2): One P; limited application.
Emerging (1): Basic point with no application.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: ‘All UK retailers should move fully online to survive.’ Evaluate this statement. Refer to at least one named UK business in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments for:
• ASOS and Ocado prove pure online works and reaches global markets.
• Lower overheads — no shop rent, fewer staff.
• Open 24/7; customer data easy to collect for targeted marketing.
• Debenhams’ refusal to move quickly is part of why it collapsed.

Arguments against:
• Primark is hugely profitable with no home delivery — its low price depends on impulse in-store buying.
• Some products need physical interaction — John Lewis’s expert service, trying on clothes, perfume testing.
• E-commerce brings high returns costs (40%+ in fashion) that can wipe out margins.
• Cyber-security and delivery issues carry real risk.
• The right answer depends on the product, the target market and the brand image — integrated mix matters more than channel.

Mastering (10–12): Sustained two-sided argument with named UK businesses (e.g. ASOS, Primark, John Lewis), clear chains of reasoning and a justified conclusion (e.g. ‘depends on target market and product type’).
Secure (7–9): Balanced argument with some application and a conclusion.
Developing (4–6): Some argument on one or both sides; limited application.
Emerging (1–3): Simple points; no real evaluation.
[12 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of a fixed cost for a small bakery?
A) The flour used to make bread
B) The electricity used per loaf baked
C) The monthly rent on the shop unit
D) The packaging for each loaf
practice_questions.marks:
C) The monthly rent on the shop unit [1 mark]
Rent does not change with the number of loaves produced; flour, electricity per loaf and packaging all vary with output.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'economies of scale'.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark: reduction in average cost as output grows / cost advantages of being larger.
2 marks: the cost advantages a business gains as it grows, reducing the average cost per unit — e.g. bulk-buying discounts or specialist machinery. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: A business has fixed costs of £4,000 and variable costs of £3 per unit. If it produces 2,000 units, calculate the average unit cost. Give your answer in £ to two decimal places.
practice_questions.marks:
Working: variable cost total = 2,000 × £3 = £6,000 (1 mark).
Total cost = £4,000 + £6,000 = £10,000 (1 mark).
Average unit cost = £10,000 ÷ 2,000 = £5.00 (1 mark for final answer with unit).
Method marks awarded for showing working even if final number is wrong. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Analyse how economies of scale could benefit a growing supermarket chain.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed chains of reasoning linking an economy of scale to a specific business benefit (e.g. purchasing → bulk discounts from milk suppliers → lower price for customers → market share grows). Applied to a supermarket chain.
Secure: Two economies identified and explained with at least one full chain.
Developing: Lists economies of scale with partial explanation.
Emerging: States economies without explaining their effects.
Indicative chains: (1) purchasing economies — bulk buying → lower per-unit input costs → higher margin or lower price → competitive advantage over smaller rivals. (2) Technical economies — specialist distribution centres and automated warehousing → lower cost per delivery → efficiency improvements. (3) Marketing economies — national advertising campaigns spread across more stores → cost per store falls. May develop one in depth. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text: A family-owned coffee chain with 12 shops is choosing between (A) expanding organically by opening new branches one at a time, or (B) buying a struggling rival chain of 15 branches in one takeover. Justify which option you would recommend.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear recommendation with two developed reasons (one fully explained), weighed against the rejected option, applied to the coffee chain with explicit reference to financing, risk, culture and economies of scale.
Secure: Clear recommendation, two developed reasons, some comparison.
Developing: Recommendation with reasons but limited weighting.
Emerging: Lists features of both without a supported choice.
Indicative content for A (organic): slower but lower risk, retains family control, each new branch learnt from carefully, cash flow manageable; but rivals may expand faster. For B (takeover): instant scale brings purchasing economies, removes a competitor, but needs a large lump sum of finance, rival sites may be loss-making, staff culture clashes, risk of diseconomies of scale. Strong answers identify the deciding factor — available finance, speed of the market, or cultural fit. [9 marks]

practice_questions.text: 'A business should always try to grow as large as possible.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should give reasoned arguments to support and challenge the statement and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments to support: economies of scale reduce average unit cost and raise profit margins; bigger firms have more bargaining power with suppliers; larger firms attract better staff and cheaper finance; market share protects against competition; brand recognition drives customer loyalty.
Arguments against: diseconomies of scale raise average unit cost when firms overstretch (parts of M&S); communication and motivation suffer in large firms; takeovers often destroy value (AOL–Time Warner); small firms can compete on quality and personal service (independent cafes, boutique brands); growth requires finance that may dilute owner control; many family firms deliberately stay small to protect culture.

Mastering: Balanced argument with developed points both sides, applied to named businesses, and a judgement introducing a new weighting (e.g. 'growth is valuable only while average unit costs keep falling and management can still communicate clearly').
Secure: Balanced argument with development both sides and a clear conclusion.
Developing: Some points either side, limited development.
Emerging: One-sided argument or list without evaluation. [12 marks]
